idiom_name: Django form/widget rendering through swappable templates (behaviour in Form/Field/Widget, markup in the project's template)
implementation_notes: Python's mainstream realization arrives through the template layer: a Django Form, Field or Widget owns the behaviour - binding, validation, ids, values - and renders through Django's template engine, where 'the form rendering process can be customized at several levels: widgets can specify custom template names; forms and widgets can specify custom renderer classes; a widget's template can be overridden by a project'. The consumer therefore supplies the markup in a template while the behaviour stays in Python and remains unit-testable without a DOM. Outside Django the same split is written by hand - a controller object exposes state plus a render hook (Textual's render(), a __rich__-style protocol, or a plain render() returning markup) and the consumer's code or template decides what appears - and because nothing re-renders automatically, the consumer must redraw after each transition.
pitfalls: Overriding template_name has no effect until the project uses a renderer that finds project templates (TemplatesSetting/Jinja2); with the default renderer the override silently falls back to the built-in template.
Reusable apps that override built-in widget templates collide with a project's custom templates - the documentation warns against it; ship a component instead.
Rendering returns safe HTML strings: composing markup in Python must follow the format_html/mark_safe rules or values are double-escaped - or, worse, marked safe unescaped.
Server-side rendering has no reactivity: every state change needs a request/re-render cycle, so primitives that assume local state do not port without a JavaScript layer.
